short_summary: A conservative thinktank and a shadow minister have called for a five-year freeze on Britain's minimum wage to stimulate youth hiring. The proposal has drawn fierce criticism from Labour over its cost to low-wage workers.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Tories call for 5-year freeze on minimum wage to tackle youth unemployment

paragraphs: A controversial proposal to halt statutory wage growth in the United Kingdom has sparked an intense economic confrontation across Westminster. A report published by the Prosperity Institute thinktank recommends freezing the national living wage at its current rate of £12.71 per hour for five consecutive years. Framed primarily as an intervention to address youth joblessness, the strategy received an explicit endorsement from Andrew Sharpe, the Conservative shadow business minister. Sharpe argued that decisive action is urgent because nearly one million young people are currently not in education, employment, or training, describing the thinktank's recommendations as sound and urging the government to adopt them in full.

Under the thinktank’s blueprint, the government would abolish the Low Pay Commission, the independent body tasked with recommending yearly wage adjustments. The report also urges ministers to return employer national insurance contributions to pre-April 2025 levels and reinstate the two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal claims—a rule previously abolished under Labour’s Employment Rights Act. The authors contend that freezing minimum pay could help roughly 270,000 young people secure employment, suggesting that for every one percentage point increase in the statutory minimum wage there is a 0.37 percentage point decrease in the youth employment rate.

However, the researchers acknowledged that they do not present these findings as costless to workers. With projected annual inflation tracking between 2% and 2.5%, the paper calculates that minimum wage earners would see their purchasing power eroded by 9% to 12% over five years. This steady erosion represents a cumulative loss of about £8,900 for low-paid workers across that period.

The proposal provoked immediate condemnation from the government. Kate Dearden, the Labour business minister, dismissed the recommendations as tin-eared, accusing the Conservative leadership under Kemi Badenoch of showing a persistent pattern of disparaging the minimum wage and being determined that the lowest-paid staff should be worse off. Dearden noted that Conservatives had opposed the minimum wage when it was initially introduced by a former Labour administration, maintaining that the current government remains committed to enhancing rights at work and giving people the breathing space they deserve on the cost of living.

The controversy underscores a broader dilemma at the top of government regarding statutory pay levels. Labour had previously promised to equalise different minimum wage tiers by granting 18- to 20-year-olds the full rate, but mounting youth unemployment has prompted debate over how rapidly to achieve that goal. Last year, the Low Pay Commission recommended a 4.1% increase in the main rate and an 8.5% rise for younger workers, bringing the two rates to £12.71 and £10.85 respectively. Ministers subsequently altered their formal guidance to the commission earlier this year, hoping to encourage a lower recommendation that might facilitate youth recruitment. However, the advisory body firmly countered that it does not believe statutory pay increases are driving higher joblessness, stating that while youth labour outcomes have deteriorated over the past two years, no robust evidence links higher youth rates to that decline. The commission will present its formal recommendations for the financial year starting April 2027 in October.

facts.fact: A report by the Prosperity Institute thinktank, endorsed by shadow business minister Andrew Sharpe, calls for a five-year freeze on the UK minimum wage at £12.71.

The report suggests freezing the wage could create around 270,000 jobs for young people, calculating that each 1 percentage point rise in the wage decreases youth employment by 0.37 percentage points.
The thinktank authors acknowledge the freeze would erode workers' purchasing power by 9% to 12% over five years, representing an £8,900 cumulative loss based on projected inflation of 2% to 2.5%.

The paper also recommends abolishing the Low Pay Commission, reversing employer national insurance contributions to pre-April 2025 levels, and reinstating the two-year qualifying period for unfair dismissal claims.
Labour business minister Kate Dearden condemned the plan as 'tin-eared', arguing it showed the Conservatives wanted the lowest-paid workers to be worse off.

The Low Pay Commission, which recommended current rates of £12.71 for adults and £10.85 for youth, stated it has found no robust evidence that higher youth rates have contributed to falling youth employment.
